text: So, we don't know what they called themselves.
We don't know their kings, their gods, or their stories.
Oddly, archaeologists haven't found grand palaces or giant royal tombs either.
Just well-planned cities built for ordinary people.
Then around 1900 BCE the great cities slowly emptied.
Why?
Nobody knows for sure.
Historians suspect a mix, rivers changing course, a river drying up, and the monsoon
growing weaker for years.
People drifted east and south into smaller villages, the drains filled with mud.
The cities were forgotten for almost 4,000 years.
And how did the world rediscover them?
Through a railway.
In the 1850s, British engineers were building a railway line in Punjab. They needed lots
of bricks. And near a village called Harappa, they found a huge pile of old perfect bricks
just lying in the ground. Sir, there's an old ruin full of bricks over there. Delighted.
Free bricks? Splendid! Old ruins never matter.
They matter. They really, really matter.
Bricks from a 4,000 year old city ended up under the tracks.
Only in the 1920s did archaeologists realise what they were digging up,
one of the oldest civilisations on earth.
So that was India's first shine, rich, organized, connected to the world.
And then its first shatter, its cities, fell silent.

But the land didn't stay empty for long.
Over the mountains in the northwest, new people were coming. They brought horses, chariots,
and a collection of hymns so sacred, it was passed down word for word, by memory alone,
for more than three thousand years. Now this one, people still argue about.
